analysis.title: Dip buying lifts US stocks after tech sell-off (UBS House View - Daily EMEA)
key_insights: US stocks rose sharply on Monday as investors returned to tech and growth shares after last week's sell-off. The S&P 500 closed 2.4% higher and the Nasdaq gained 2.7%. The rebound continued in Asia on Tuesday, with AI-heavy indices in South Korea, Japan and Taiwan up between 2% and 4%.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose 6.9%, while NVIDIA fell 4.3% after the start of an internal investigation into its CEO Jensen Huang. Most S&P 500 sectors advanced, with consumer discretionary and communication services among the strongest. Airlines and cruise operators gained on lower expected fuel costs.

Brent crude is down 7% this week to near USD 91 a barrel and WTI has fallen toward USD 85/bbl on hopes for progress in US-Iran diplomacy. Lower energy costs have eased near-term inflation concerns ahead of Tuesday's US CPI report.

UBS reads the rebound as dip buying and a reversal of part of last week's de-risking. The chip and AI infrastructure decline was amplified by elevated positioning, high expectations and uncertainty over data center development. UBS calls the sell-off a positioning reset, not the start of a lasting downturn in the AI investment cycle.

The breadth of Monday's rally supports the view that investors are differentiating between companies and parts of the AI ecosystem, not reassessing the broader outlook for growth and earnings. Last week's weakness was concentrated in chips, data-center companies and highly valued growth stocks.

UBS says underlying AI demand remains robust, citing accelerating cloud revenue and growing advance orders for computing capacity. It forecasts aggregate AI capital spending of USD 1.0tr in 2026, USD 1.4tr in 2027 and USD 1.5tr in 2028. Political and physical constraints may delay, relocate or raise the cost of data-center projects but are unlikely to eliminate demand.

Risks remain. Investors increasingly want evidence that rising AI spending will generate sustainable revenue, utilization and returns. Concentrated positioning leaves individual companies sensitive to guidance, regulation, financing conditions and sentiment, and UBS says further tech volatility would not be surprising.

The physical oil market remains vulnerable after earlier supply disruptions and inventory drawdowns. Diplomatic progress could push prices lower, while renewed attacks or a breakdown in talks could quickly reverse the move.

Tuesday's US October CPI report is the next test. Strong October employment data have kept alive expectations for a December Fed rate increase. A stronger-than-expected reading could lift bond yields and challenge the equity rebound. Contained price pressures would support expectations for a measured tightening cycle.

UBS sees potential gains in broad equity indices over the next six to 12 months, backed by resilient earnings and growth. Its three portfolio suggestions are: manage concentration risk, rebalance across sectors and regions, and build a multi-asset core.

On concentration, UBS says investors should keep exposure to the structural AI theme but use strength to trim oversized single-stock tech positions. It favors established technology platforms with existing computing capacity, visible AI revenues, strong balance sheets and the ability to fund investment internally.
On sectors and regions, UBS prefers US industrials and health care and the Eurozone, where it expects 2027 earnings growth similar to the US but at lower valuations.

On multi-asset, UBS suggests rebuilding strategic allocations for investors with large bond underweights, favoring high quality short- and medium-term bonds. Alternatives and broad commodity exposure can add return and hedge geopolitical or inflation shocks.
